paragraphs.heading: Making more viruses
paragraphs.text: Viral replication is how new viruses are made inside the cells a virus infects. A virus can multiply only within a living cell, and it has to get inside first. By turning out many copies of its genes and packing them up, it goes on to infect new hosts. The host cell pays for all of it, supplying the energy, the building machinery and the small raw materials for viral proteins and nucleic acids.

paragraphs.heading: Step one, attachment
paragraphs.text: The process starts when a virus latches on to a host cell. Often it does so with an attachment protein that sticks out from its protein shell, the capsid. That protein binds a receptor on the cell's outer membrane. Viruses can take advantage of a receptor's normal job by mimicking the molecules that usually bind it. The rhinovirus, for example, grips a receptor called ICAM-1, which cells normally use to stick to one another.

paragraphs.heading: Step two, getting in
paragraphs.text: Next the virus crosses the cell's outer membrane, a step called entry or penetration. The most common route is receptor-mediated endocytosis: the virus binds a receptor, chemical signals follow, and the cell folds its membrane around the virus to form a small bubble, or vesicle, inside the cell. This costs the virus no energy, only the host. In other cases, proteins on the outside of the virus make it fuse with the membrane, which opens a pore; once inside, the virus sheds its coat and its genes move into the cytoplasm.

paragraphs.heading: Step three, uncoating
paragraphs.text: Once inside, the virus loses its protein coat and lets its genetic material out, a step called uncoating. Viruses do this in different ways. Rhinoviruses use the low pH inside the cell's endosomes to trigger it, releasing a protein that punches holes so the genome can escape. Many DNA viruses instead travel to the nucleus and pass their genes in through its pores.

paragraphs.heading: Step four, copying the genome
paragraphs.text: The fourth step is replication proper, the fast production of the viral genome. How it goes depends on what kind of genetic material the virus has, since each kind takes over the matching machinery in the cell. Viruses with double-stranded DNA share their kind of genetic material with all living things, so they can use the copying enzymes in the cell's nucleus. Many RNA viruses copy themselves in the cytosol and reach the cell's ribosomes directly to make viral proteins.

paragraphs.heading: Two ways to live in a cell
paragraphs.text: Viruses can follow one of two life cycles. In the lytic cycle, the virus puts its genome into the cell and starts copying by taking over the cell's machinery to make new viruses. In the lysogenic cycle, the viral genome is built into the host's own genome and is copied each time the cell divides. Later, chemical or environmental triggers can wake it up and start virus production.
